seo.title: CodeBuddy vs HagiCode: Features and Comparison
seo.description: CodeBuddy Code is Tencent's terminal AI coding agent; HagiCode is a workbench that runs it. Compare install, pricing, features and fit.

summary: CodeBuddy Code is Tencent Cloud's terminal coding agent, installed from npm, Homebrew or a native binary. HagiCode is a desktop workbench that runs CodeBuddy as its executor and adds parallel sessions, proposals and AI commits around it.

content: CodeBuddy Code is the command-line coding agent from Tencent Cloud's CodeBuddy product line, which also includes an IDE and editor plugins. HagiCode is a desktop and web workbench that runs CodeBuddy as one of its executors. It does not replace CodeBuddy and does not host models.

If you want an agent in your terminal, you use your CodeBuddy account, and you work on one task at a time, CodeBuddy alone is enough. HagiCode is for the point where you want several CodeBuddy tasks running side by side, written proposals before code changes, or one workspace across several repositories.

sections.title: CodeBuddy vs HagiCode at a glance

cells: What it is
Terminal AI coding agent from Tencent Cloud; sibling products are the CodeBuddy IDE and editor plugins
Desktop and web workbench that runs Agent CLIs, CodeBuddy among them; not a model or an agent itself
Interface and platforms
Terminal, with -p for scripted runs; native binary for macOS, Linux and Windows (beta), or npm and Homebrew
Desktop app for Windows, macOS and Linux; Docker Compose container; Microsoft Store edition
Pricing and licensing
Free, Pro (about $10 per month) and Team (about $40 per seat) plans, credit-based; as of October 2026, per Tencent Cloud's billing page
Desktop and Container editions are free; Store edition is free with an optional one-time TurboEngine purchase
Model and provider access
Models come with your CodeBuddy account and site; extra models via models.json with an OpenAI-compatible endpoint
Hosts no models; uses whatever your CodeBuddy install is signed in to; optional OmniRoute model catalog
Parallel work
Sub-agents inside a session, and Agent Teams exposed over ACP
Several sessions side by side, each an Agent with a visible status
Spec and planning workflow
Plan permission mode, /init for project context, hooks and skills
OpenSpec proposals: propose, validate, apply, archive; free editions allow 3 concurrent proposals
Git and commit handling
Built-in Git operations; can generate commit messages in the terminal
AI-composed commits, repository locked while committing, per-repo targeting with Monospecs
Setup effort
One npm, Homebrew or script install, then sign in to the China, International or enterprise site
Needs CodeBuddy installed and signed in first, then HagiCode Desktop on top
Best for
Terminal users in Tencent Cloud's ecosystem, scripts and CI
Parallel tasks, proposal-driven work and multi-repo projects

items.title: Several install routes
content: CodeBuddy Code installs with `npm install -g @tencent-ai/codebuddy-code` (Node.js 18.20 or later), or through Homebrew with `brew install Tencent-CodeBuddy/tap/codebuddy-code`. Homebrew does not need Node.js, and a beta native binary does not either, and `codebuddy install` migrates an npm install to it.
The command is `codebuddy` (the docs also mention a `cbc` alias); check it with `codebuddy --version`. `codebuddy update` upgrades it, and auto-update is on by default.

items.title: Sign-in by region and by organisation
content: On first launch you choose where to sign in: the China site, the International site, an enterprise domain for dedicated deployments, or iOA for Tencent staff. The China and International sites expose different model sets, so check which one your account belongs to before comparing models.

items.title: Scriptable and permission-aware
content: `codebuddy -p` runs a single prompt and accepts piped input, so it works in shell pipelines, for example `cat error.log | codebuddy -p "..."`. Shift+Tab cycles permission modes (default, bypass, accept edits, plan), and `-y` skips confirmations for runs that need file or command access.

items.title: Extensibility and enterprise reach
content: Docs cover MCP servers, sub-agents, plugins, skills, hooks, Python and TypeScript SDKs, GitHub Actions and a web UI. Models can be added in `~/.codebuddy/models.json` or per project, and enterprise deployments can run in containers. `codebuddy --acp` exposes it as an ACP server with a context-window option and Agent Teams status, which is the interface HagiCode uses.

sections.title: When to choose CodeBuddy, and when to choose HagiCode

items: you work in a terminal and one task at a time is enough;
you are already in Tencent Cloud's ecosystem or on an enterprise CodeBuddy domain;
you want scripted runs with `codebuddy -p`, piped input or GitHub Actions;
you want the lightest route: a Homebrew or native-binary install with no extra application;
you prefer its own permission modes, hooks and plugins to a separate workbench.
you run several CodeBuddy tasks at once and want them in one view;
you want a reviewed proposal before the agent edits code, archived afterwards;
a CodeBuddy task needs edits in more than one repository and you want to plan it once;
you want CodeBuddy's changes committed with generated messages, without leaving the window for an editor;
you use CodeBuddy alongside other Agent CLIs and want one workspace.

blocks.title: Where HagiCode is not the right tool
content: Scripts and CI runs should call `codebuddy -p` directly; a desktop workbench adds nothing there.
If you only want a terminal, or you have one quick question and an editor already open, HagiCode is more than you need.

HagiCode needs CodeBuddy installed and signed in first, so setup is longer than using CodeBuddy alone. Teams that do not want a proposal discipline will find it overhead, free editions cap concurrent proposals at 3, and the embedded Code Server editor is not a full IDE replacement.
CodeBuddy's own IDE and editor plugins are separate products; HagiCode drives only the CLI.
HagiCode sits on top of the CLI. It starts your CodeBuddy install over ACP, so your account, region and credits stay with CodeBuddy and HagiCode does not take over its sign-in.
Nothing is locked in. Your repositories and your `.codebuddy` settings stay where they are, and you can run `codebuddy` on the same project whenever you like.

items: Install CodeBuddy Code with npm, Homebrew or the native installer, and confirm it with `codebuddy --version`.
Run `codebuddy` once and sign in on the site that matches your account (China, International or enterprise).
Install HagiCode Desktop for Windows, macOS or Linux, or use the Docker Compose or Microsoft Store edition.
In HagiCode's Agent CLI settings, pick CodeBuddy as the executor; HagiCode looks for the `codebuddy` command on your PATH.
Open a repository and start a session or an OpenSpec proposal; CodeBuddy's tool calls appear in HagiCode's unified view.
To go back, close HagiCode and run `codebuddy` in the same folder; nothing needs to be undone.

blocks.title: What works with CodeBuddy inside HagiCode
content: Parallel sessions, Agents management, OpenSpec proposals, AI commits, Code Server, Monospecs, Vault and the unified tool-call view work with CodeBuddy sessions.

Interactive questions are available only for Claude, Pi, OMP and Reasonix, and the agent work panel only for Claude Code, so neither appears for CodeBuddy. Which models you can pick depends on the site you signed in to.

sections.title: What HagiCode adds on top of any agent

items.title: Parallel sessions and Agents management
content: Each CodeBuddy session becomes an Agent with its own context and a status you can scan, instead of one more terminal running `codebuddy`. That helps most when you start tasks across several folders.

items.title: OpenSpec proposals
content: A task can begin as an OpenSpec proposal you write, validate, apply and archive. CodeBuddy implements within it, and the proposal keeps the reasoning that a terminal scrollback loses.

items.title: AI commit and Code Server
content: HagiCode drafts the commit message from CodeBuddy's changes and locks the repository while it commits. The embedded Code Server editor opens the files CodeBuddy touched next to the conversation.

items.title: Monospecs and Vault
content: Monospecs lists the repositories of a multi-repo workspace so a CodeBuddy task sees all of them. Vault keeps reference projects and notes available to later sessions, including those started in a fresh `codebuddy` process.

items.title: Model routing, tool-call view and usage
content: CodeBuddy's tool calls are shown in the same typed shape as every other CLI, live and in history. OmniRoute can supply a model catalog per Agent CLI, and an optional TokenMonitor readout in the status bar shows today's tokens and cost.

items: CodeBuddy Code is the agent in your terminal; HagiCode is the workbench that runs it.
Use CodeBuddy alone for solo, single-task or scripted work; add HagiCode for parallel tasks, proposals and multi-repo changes.
CodeBuddy must be installed and signed in first, and you can go back to running `codebuddy` directly at any time.

faq.question: How do I install CodeBuddy Code?
faq.answer: Run `npm install -g @tencent-ai/codebuddy-code` (Node.js 18.20 or later), or on macOS and Linux `brew install Tencent-CodeBuddy/tap/codebuddy-code`. A beta native binary needs no Node.js. Then run `codebuddy --version` and `codebuddy` to sign in. See the docs at codebuddy.ai/docs/cli/installation.

faq.question: Is CodeBuddy free?
faq.answer: CodeBuddy has a free plan with a small monthly credit allowance, plus Pro and Team plans (Pro about $10 per month, Team about $40 per seat, as of October 2026). Tencent Cloud's billing page does not say which plans include the CLI, so check it before relying on the free tier.

faq.question: Can I use CodeBuddy with HagiCode?
faq.answer: Yes. Install and sign in to CodeBuddy Code, then choose it as the Agent CLI in HagiCode. HagiCode drives it over ACP, and your account and credits stay with CodeBuddy.

faq.question: Does HagiCode replace CodeBuddy?
faq.answer: No. HagiCode runs CodeBuddy as its executor and adds sessions, proposals, commits and multi-repo tools around it. You can still run `codebuddy` on the same repositories.

faq.question: What is the CodeBuddy command?
faq.answer: The command is `codebuddy`, with `cbc` mentioned as a short alias in the docs. The npm package is @tencent-ai/codebuddy-code.

faq.question: CodeBuddy vs HagiCode: which should I pick?
faq.answer: Pick CodeBuddy alone for terminal, solo or scripted work. Add HagiCode when you want parallel sessions, OpenSpec proposals or multi-repo workspaces on top of CodeBuddy.
